weeks.title: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
weeks.theme: Nothing improves until it is measured honestly. This week you write down exactly where you are — including the parts that are embarrassing — and start the language work everything else sits on. No AI writes a line of code for you. That rule is the whole point.
weeks.deliverable: A public GitHub repository named backend-mastery containing LOG.md (one honest paragraph per day), week-01/ with every exercise you wrote by hand, and BASELINE.md recording your starting scores.
weeks.milestone: Six consecutive days with at least one commit. Baseline recorded for: LeetCode Easy solved unaided, JavaScript self-quiz score, and one honest sentence naming what you actually built in three years.

dsa.topic: Arrays & hashing

weeks.title: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword
weeks.theme: Closures are the most common intermediate JavaScript interview question, and "this" is the one people three years in still get wrong. Both are the same idea: a function carries context with it. Get this week right and a whole category of questions stops being frightening.
weeks.deliverable: week-02/ containing a counter factory, a private-variable module, a memoisation wrapper, and a written explanation of the var-in-a-loop problem in your own words.
weeks.milestone: You can define a closure out loud, unaided, in one sentence, and produce a working example from a blank file in under five minutes.

dsa.topic: Arrays & hashing

weeks.title: Arrays, Objects, and Reading Errors Like an Engineer
weeks.theme: The array and object methods that appear in nearly every screening test, and the debugger — because the fastest way to look like a three-year engineer is to read a stack trace correctly instead of guessing.
weeks.deliverable: week-03/ containing an order-analysis script built with map/filter/reduce, and a written record of four bugs you introduced deliberately and fixed using only the debugger.
weeks.milestone: You can use reduce correctly from memory, and you can set a breakpoint, step into a call, and read the call stack without looking anything up.

dsa.topic: Arrays & hashing

weeks.title: The Event Loop, Promises, and the Paperwork Gate + Git Properly, and the First Applications
weeks.theme:
Async is where self-taught confidence collapses, and it is asked in every backend interview you will sit. In parallel the paperwork has to finish this week, because applications open on Monday and a gate that slips is a gate that never closes.

Applications open — three a week, every one tailored. Three is deliberately small: at this stage each application is a test of the CV, not a lottery ticket. The engineering half is Git, which you have used for three years and do not actually understand.
weeks.deliverable: CV version one as a real PDF, a rewritten LinkedIn profile, a GitHub profile with a README and no empty repositories, and week-04/ with hand-written promise exercises. · ALSO: Three tailored applications logged in APPLICATIONS.md, and a practice repository where you have created and resolved a merge conflict, rebased a branch, and recovered a lost commit from the reflog.
weeks.milestone: GATE — CV, LinkedIn and GitHub finished by Saturday 17 October. Not "nearly". A stranger can find you, read one page, and know what you do. And you can explain the event loop out loud in ninety seconds. · AND: Three applications out. You can explain the difference between merge and rebase, and what git reset --hard actually destroys, without looking it up.

dsa.topic: Hash maps — frequency & lookup → Two pointers

weeks.title: OOP and SOLID — The Shape NestJS Assumes + TypeScript for Backend Engineers
weeks.theme:
NestJS is an opinionated object-oriented framework built on dependency injection. If classes, interfaces and inversion of control are vague to you, Nest will feel like magic and you will never debug it confidently. This week removes the magic before you meet it.

TypeScript is not optional at the tier you are targeting, and NestJS is built on its decorators and metadata. This week is types that carry weight — generics, narrowing, and the compiler settings that actually catch bugs — plus the decorator mechanics Nest depends on.
weeks.deliverable: week-06/ containing a small library system modelled in classes, refactored so the storage mechanism can be swapped without touching business logic, plus your own hand-written dependency-injection container in about thirty lines. · ALSO: The expense tracker ported to strict TypeScript with no any, plus a worked file demonstrating decorators and metadata reflection from first principles.
weeks.milestone: You can explain dependency inversion with an example from your own code, and you have written a DI container yourself — so Nest's providers will be obvious rather than magical. · AND: BLOCK I CLOSES. You can type a function, an object and a generic without help, you know what strict mode turns on, and you can explain what a decorator is at runtime.

dsa.topic: Two pointers — sorted arrays → Sliding window — fixed size

weeks.title: The Node Runtime — Modules, npm, Process + Node Internals — Event Loop Phases, Streams, Buffers
weeks.theme:
You have written server code for three years without knowing what the runtime does. This week is modules, resolution, the standard library and the process itself — the ground everything else stands on.

The week that separates you from every other candidate who says "Node is non-blocking" and cannot go further. Libuv phases, the thread pool, streams and backpressure, and what a Buffer actually is.
weeks.deliverable: week-08/ containing a three-module project built by hand in both CommonJS and ESM, a directory-walker using fs and path correctly, and a script that fails properly with a non-zero exit code. · ALSO: week-09/ containing a measured demonstration of a blocked event loop, a stream pipeline that processes a file larger than memory, and a written explanation of backpressure in your own words.
weeks.milestone: You can explain module resolution, the difference between CommonJS and ESM, and what an unhandled rejection does to a Node process. · AND: You can name the event loop phases in order, explain what runs in the thread pool and what does not, and demonstrate backpressure with code you wrote.

dsa.topic: Sliding window — variable size → Strings — parsing & building

weeks.title: Express — Routing, Middleware, the Request Lifecycle + REST API Design a Reviewer Would Approve
weeks.theme:
Express is small enough to understand completely, and understanding it completely is what lets you answer the most common backend interview question at this level: what happens between the request arriving and the response leaving.

Anyone can make an endpoint return JSON. This week is the decisions a reviewer looks at: resource naming, status codes, pagination, filtering, idempotency, versioning, and what your API does when the client sends nonsense.
weeks.deliverable: week-10/ containing an Express server with a hand-written middleware stack — request id, logging, timing, body limit, auth check, central error handler — every one written by you, and a diagram of the request lifecycle drawn by you. · ALSO: The Project 1 API with two resources, full CRUD, pagination, filtering, a single documented error shape, and an OpenAPI document that matches the implementation.
weeks.milestone: You can draw the path of a request through an Express app from memory, including where errors go and why middleware order is not cosmetic. · AND: You can defend every status code your API returns, and explain cursor versus offset pagination and when each breaks.

dsa.topic: Strings — anagrams & palindromes → Prefix sums

weeks.title: Validation, Error Handling, Logging + Deploy It — The API Goes Public
weeks.theme:
The unglamorous week that separates a project that looks like a tutorial from one that looks like production. None of it is hard and all of it is visible to a reviewer within thirty seconds of opening your repository.

A deployed thing you can link to changes every conversation you have from here on. It is not finished and that is the point: deploy early, deploy badly, learn what breaks, and then have a URL on your CV for the remaining thirty-seven weeks.
weeks.deliverable: Project 1 with schema validation on every input, a real error taxonomy with custom error classes, and structured logging where a request id flows through every log line for one request. · ALSO: PROJECT 1 API DEPLOYED at a public URL over HTTPS, with a health check, environment-based configuration, and a README a stranger can follow.
weeks.milestone: You can trace a single request end to end through your logs by its id, and you can explain the difference between an operational error and a programmer error. · AND: ANCHOR — the API is reachable from the public internet on Saturday 15 November. Application quota rises to five a week because the CV now points at something running.

dsa.topic: Matrix traversal → Stacks — monotonic & matching

weeks.title: SQL I — Selects, Joins, Thinking in Sets + SQL II — Window Functions and the Hard Queries
weeks.theme:
You have written SQL for three years and most of it was generated. SQL is the highest-return subject in this book: asked in almost every interview, testable in fifteen minutes, and being genuinely good at it is rare enough to be a differentiator.

The second SQL week, and the one that makes you unusual. Window functions are asked at tier 2, rarely known at tier 4, and they turn a category of "impossible without application code" questions into four lines.
weeks.deliverable: A seeded PostgreSQL practice database of five related tables and a few thousand rows, plus forty solved exercises written by hand with no AI and no copied answers. · ALSO: week-15/ containing thirty more solved exercises covering window functions, ranking, running totals, gaps and islands, and set operations.
weeks.milestone: You can write a three-table join with grouping and a having clause from a blank editor, first try, without looking up the syntax. · AND: You can produce a per-group top-N query and a running total with a window function, from memory, and explain what the frame clause does.

dsa.topic: Queues & deques → Linked lists — traversal & reversal

weeks.title: Schema Design and Normalization + PostgreSQL in Depth
weeks.theme:
Design questions separate three-year engineers from each other. Anyone can query a schema someone else designed. This week is designing one that does not have to be rescued in eighteen months.

PostgreSQL specifically, not "a database". Types that prevent bugs, JSONB for the genuinely schemaless parts, psql instead of a GUI, and the features that make Postgres the default answer at the companies you are targeting.
weeks.deliverable: A designed, documented and migrated schema for Project 1 — entities, relationships, keys, constraints — with a written justification for every denormalisation you chose. · ALSO: Project 1 using correct Postgres types throughout, one justified JSONB column with an index on it, and a written note on every type choice you changed and why.
weeks.milestone: Given a described business problem you can produce a normalised schema on paper in twenty minutes and defend each decision. · AND: You can use psql without a GUI, and you can explain why timestamptz and numeric exist and what goes wrong without them.

dsa.topic: Linked lists — cycle & merge → Binary search — exact match

weeks.title: Indexes and Query Plans + Transactions and Concurrency — and AI Comes Back
weeks.theme:
The single most valuable week in the plan for your market position. Very few three-year candidates in this market can honestly say "I read query plans". After this week you can, with numbers from your own project.

Transactions separate a developer from an engineer in a backend interview. Two users buying the last item at the same moment is a question you will be asked, and the answer is not "I would check the stock first". Also: on Monday, AI returns as a reviewer.
weeks.deliverable: A written before-and-after for five queries you indexed, with the EXPLAIN ANALYZE output for each and the timing difference. · ALSO: week-19/ containing a demonstrated lost-update race condition and three different correct fixes, each with the SQL and a written explanation of its trade-off.
weeks.milestone: You can read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan, say which line is the problem, and predict whether an index will help before you create it. · AND: ANCHOR — AI unlocked on Monday 1 December, as reviewer and teacher, never author. And you can describe a race condition you personally reproduced.

dsa.topic: Binary search — on the answer → Sorting — custom comparators

weeks.title: ORMs — Prisma and TypeORM + MongoDB and Modelling Without Joins
weeks.theme:
Every team you interview with uses an ORM, and the useful answer to "why not raw SQL" is one you can only give having done both. You have written six weeks of SQL by hand; now learn what an ORM buys and what it quietly costs.

NoSQL is not "SQL but easier", it is a different modelling discipline: you design around your queries instead of around your entities. Knowing when a document store is genuinely right — and saying so honestly — is worth more in an interview than knowing its syntax.
weeks.deliverable: Project 1 on Prisma, with three queries deliberately left in raw SQL and a comment on each saying why, plus a written comparison of Prisma and TypeORM from having used both. · ALSO: A second copy of one Project 1 domain modelled in MongoDB, with the aggregation pipeline equivalents of three of your SQL reports, and a written argument for which store you would actually choose.
weeks.milestone: You can name three things an ORM makes worse, not just three it makes better. And you can reproduce and fix an N+1 query on demand. · AND: You can explain embedding versus referencing with a rule for choosing, and you can write an aggregation pipeline with $match, $group and $lookup from memory.

dsa.topic: Intervals — merge & overlap → Trees — DFS traversal

weeks.title: Replication, Partitioning, Sharding — and the Block Close + NestJS Fundamentals — Modules, Controllers, Providers, DI
weeks.theme:
The scaling vocabulary. You will not shard anything this year, and you will be asked about it, because the question tests whether you understand the trade-offs rather than whether you have operated one.

The architecture, and why it exists. Nest is Angular's structure applied to the server: modules that declare what they own, providers resolved by a container, and controllers that do nothing but translate HTTP. You built a crude version of this in week 6; now see it done properly.
weeks.deliverable: A working local replica of your Postgres database with reads served from it, one partitioned table with a demonstrated pruning benefit, and a written scaling path for Project 1 from one server to many. · ALSO: PROJECT 2 started — the Nest skeleton of your Project 1 domain, with two feature modules, controllers, services and repositories, wired by DI, and a written comparison against your own week-6 container.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK III CLOSES — ANCHOR: Project 1 has a complete, indexed, transactional data layer across SQL and NoSQL by Saturday 19 December. You can explain replication lag and why it breaks read-after-write. · AND: You can explain what the Nest DI container does at startup, what a provider token is, and why a circular dependency between two modules happens — without calling any of it magic.

dsa.topic: Trees — BFS by level → Binary search trees

weeks.title: The Request Pipeline — Pipes, Guards, Interceptors, Filters + The Nest Data Layer — TypeORM, Prisma, Transactions
weeks.theme:
Nest's request pipeline is Express middleware with names and ordering guarantees. Knowing the exact order — middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, handler, interceptors again, filters — is the single most asked Nest interview question.

Connecting Block III to Block IV. The repository pattern Nest assumes, migrations that run in CI, and transactions that span services — which is the part every tutorial skips and every real system needs.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with a validation pipe on every DTO, a guard protecting one route, a logging interceptor adding timing, and a global exception filter producing your standard error shape. · ALSO: Project 2 on a real database with entities, migrations, a repository layer behind interfaces, and one multi-service operation wrapped in a single transaction.
weeks.milestone: You can draw the Nest request pipeline in order from memory and say what each stage is for and what it must not do. · AND: You can explain how a transaction spans two services in Nest without passing a connection object through every method signature.

dsa.topic: Trees — path & depth problems → Heaps — top K

weeks.title: Authentication and Authorisation in Nest + Testing — Unit, Integration, End to End
weeks.theme:
Auth is the most commonly implemented and most commonly implemented-badly part of a backend, and a favourite interview subject because the wrong answers are so recognisable. Build it properly once, in Nest, and understand every trade-off you chose.

You have never written a test. At tier 2 that is disqualifying, and it is the easiest gap in this book to close: one week of real tests on a project you already understand changes how your repository reads to a reviewer.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with registration, login, refresh, logout, role-based authorisation on at least two routes, and a written justification of the session-versus-token decision. · ALSO: A real test suite on Project 2 — unit tests on business logic, integration tests on the repository layer against a throwaway database, e2e tests on every endpoint — running green from a clean checkout.
weeks.milestone: You can explain why a JWT in localStorage is a risk, what refresh-token rotation solves, and how you log a user out of a stateless system. Nobody at this level should be guessing here. · AND: The suite runs green from empty, covers every endpoint at least once including failure paths, and you can explain what you deliberately chose not to test.

dsa.topic: Heaps — streaming median → Recursion — the base-case habit

weeks.title: GraphQL and WebSockets in Nest + The Work That Happens Later — Uploads, Email, Cron, Microservices
weeks.theme:
Two protocols beyond REST that appear constantly in job descriptions at this tier. Neither is hard once you have REST properly; both are asked about, and having shipped each once is the difference between an opinion and an answer.

The last Nest week. Everything a real service does besides answer requests: accept files, send email, run scheduled work, and talk to other services. Plus Nest's microservice transports, so you can speak about distributed systems from having touched one.
weeks.deliverable: A GraphQL layer over part of the Project 2 domain with a solved N+1 via DataLoader, and a WebSocket gateway pushing live updates to connected clients. · ALSO: Project 2 with pre-signed direct file upload, transactional email, two scheduled jobs that are safe to run on multiple instances, and one module extracted into a separate microservice.
weeks.milestone: You can explain the N+1 problem in GraphQL specifically and how DataLoader batches it, and you can say when WebSockets are the wrong choice. · AND: BLOCK IV CLOSES. You can explain why a cron job on three instances runs three times and the three ways to stop it — which is a question that catches most candidates.

dsa.topic: Backtracking — subsets → Backtracking — permutations

weeks.title: Redis and Caching Strategies + Queues, Workers and Message Brokers
weeks.theme:
Caching is easy to add and hard to invalidate, and "cache invalidation" jokes are told by people who have never had to do it. This week is Redis as a real data structure server, and caching as a decision with a written invalidation strategy.

The moment a request does work the user should not wait for, you need a queue — and the moment you have a queue you need to think about retries, failures and ordering. This is the backbone of every serious backend and it is where system design interviews go.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with a measured cache on its most expensive read path, a written invalidation strategy, and Redis-backed sessions and WebSocket fan-out. · ALSO: Project 2 with a real job queue and a separate worker process, retries with backoff, a dead-letter queue, and one event-driven flow where a write publishes an event that two handlers consume.
weeks.milestone: You can name four caching strategies and say which one you used and why, and you can describe a cache stampede and how you would prevent it. · AND: You can explain at-least-once versus at-most-once delivery, why idempotent consumers are mandatory, and what a dead-letter queue is for.

dsa.topic: Graphs — build the adjacency list → Graphs — BFS shortest path

weeks.title: Rate Limiting, API Gateways and Resilience + Ship Project 2
weeks.theme:
Protecting a service from its callers, and from its own dependencies. Rate limiting, circuit breakers, timeouts and retries — the difference between a service that degrades and one that falls over and takes its neighbours with it.

A finished project is one a stranger can use, understand and evaluate without you in the room. This week is the last ten per cent, which is always more than ten per cent — and at the end you have two shipped backend services, which is two more than most candidates.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 with a Redis-backed distributed rate limiter, timeouts and a circuit breaker on every outbound call, and a written note on what the service does when each dependency is unavailable. · ALSO: PROJECT 2 LIVE — deployed, documented, with a demo account, an architecture diagram, a two-minute demo video, and the measured numbers from weeks 18, 28, 30 and 31 in the README.
weeks.milestone: You can explain the difference between a fixed window, a sliding window and a token bucket, and why an in-memory rate limiter is wrong the moment you run two instances. · AND: ANCHOR — Project 2 live by Saturday 24 January. A NestJS service with a real data layer, auth, queues, caching, real-time and tests, running at a public URL.

dsa.topic: Graphs — DFS & connected components → Graphs — topological sort

weeks.title: Linux and the Shell + Docker and Docker Compose
weeks.theme:
Every server you will touch is Linux and every pipeline is a shell script. You have avoided both for three years. One week to stop being a tourist on the command line.

Containers are the vocabulary of every infrastructure conversation you will have. The goal is not memorising commands — it is understanding images, layers and networking well enough to debug when it does not work.
weeks.deliverable: week-34/ containing a backup script that dumps a database, compresses, rotates anything older than seven days, logs every step and exits non-zero on failure — plus a successful restore from it. · ALSO: Project 2 fully containerised — a multi-stage Dockerfile under 200MB running as a non-root user, and a compose file bringing up API, worker, Postgres and Redis with one command.
weeks.milestone: You can diagnose a Linux box over SSH with no GUI: what is listening, what is eating memory, what filled the disk, what the logs say. · AND: A stranger can clone Project 2 and run the whole stack with one command, and you can explain the difference between an image and a container without hedging.

dsa.topic: Graphs — cycle detection → Union-find

weeks.title: Nginx, TLS, DNS and the Network + CI/CD with GitHub Actions
weeks.theme:
What sits in front of your service, and how a request actually reaches it. Reverse proxying, certificates, DNS and the network layer — all of it asked about, most of it never learned properly by people who deploy to a platform that hides it.

Tests nobody runs are documentation. This week the tests run on every push, the image builds in the pipeline, and deployment stops being something you do by hand at eleven at night.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 behind Nginx on a domain you own, with a real certificate that auto-renews, gzip, correct proxy headers, and a written trace of a request from DNS lookup to response. · ALSO: A GitHub Actions pipeline on Project 2: lint, test against a service database, build and push the image, deploy on merge to main — with branch protection that blocks a red build.
weeks.milestone: You can explain what happens between typing a URL and receiving a response, including DNS, TCP, TLS and the proxy — end to end, from memory. · AND: A pull request with a failing test cannot be merged, and deployment happens on merge rather than by hand.

dsa.topic: Greedy — interval scheduling → DP — 1D, climbing & house robber

weeks.title: Jenkins + AWS Foundations — IAM, EC2, S3
weeks.theme:
A large number of Pakistani employers run Jenkins, often self-hosted and inherited. GitHub Actions teaches you pipelines; Jenkins teaches you the version of pipelines that a real company asks you to maintain. Knowing both is a hiring advantage.

You have the certificate and have never built anything. This week gives it evidence: identity, a server you configured, and object storage wired into your own application.
weeks.deliverable: A Jenkins instance running in Docker with a declarative Jenkinsfile in the Project 2 repository — checkout, install, lint, test against a database, build the image, deploy on main — plus credentials handled properly and one shared library function. · ALSO: An AWS account locked down with MFA and least-privilege users, a billing alarm, Project 2 running on EC2, and S3 handling uploads through pre-signed URLs with public access blocked.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK VI CLOSES. The same pipeline exists twice, in Actions and in Jenkins, and you can compare them from experience rather than opinion. · AND: You can explain the difference between an IAM user, a role and a policy, and why an application should use a role rather than an access key.

dsa.topic: DP — 1D, coin change → DP — 2D grids

weeks.title: Networking and Managed Data — VPC, RDS, ELB, Auto Scaling + Containers and Serverless on AWS — ECS, EKS, Lambda, SQS
weeks.theme:
The part of AWS that is actually architecture. A private network, a managed database that is not reachable from the internet, a load balancer in front, and a group that replaces an instance when it dies.

Where your Docker work meets the cloud. ECS for running containers without operating Kubernetes, enough EKS to hold the conversation, Lambda for the work that suits it, and SQS because your queue should not depend on one Redis box.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 on a VPC you designed — public and private subnets, RDS in private with no public access, an application load balancer in front, and an auto-scaling group of at least two instances. · ALSO: Project 2 running on ECS Fargate — API and worker as separate services behind the load balancer, secrets from Secrets Manager, and one queue moved to SQS with a dead-letter queue.
weeks.milestone: You can draw your own VPC from memory and explain the path of a packet from the internet to the database and back. · AND: You can explain when you would choose ECS over EKS over Lambda, in terms of what each costs you rather than what each is called.

dsa.topic: DP — subsequences → DP — knapsack

weeks.title: Observability — CloudWatch, Prometheus, Grafana + LLM Fundamentals and Prompt Engineering
weeks.theme:
You cannot operate what you cannot see. Logs you can search, metrics that mean something, dashboards that answer a question, and exactly one alarm that wakes you up — because an alert nobody acts on trains you to ignore alerts.

Not a course on AI. A working understanding of tokens, context, cost and failure modes, so that Project 3 is engineering rather than incantation — and so you answer AI questions like a backend engineer rather than a user.
weeks.deliverable: Project 2 exporting application metrics to Prometheus, a Grafana dashboard answering four real questions, logs searchable in CloudWatch, and one alarm on a symptom that reaches your phone. · ALSO: PROJECT3.md with a one-paragraph scope and a chosen document set, plus a working API integration with token accounting, a hard cost ceiling, retries and a measured cost per request.
weeks.milestone: BLOCK VII CLOSES. You can answer "how do you know the service is healthy?" by opening a dashboard rather than describing an intention. · AND: You can state Project 3's cost per thousand requests, and explain what a token is and why a context window is a constraint rather than a feature.

dsa.topic: DP — recognising the pattern cold → Mixed mediums — timed

weeks.title: Embeddings, Vector Search and RAG + Agents, MCP, and Ship Project 3
weeks.theme:
Retrieval is a search problem wearing new clothes, and the engineering is the unglamorous half: chunking, indexing, and evaluating whether what you retrieved was any good. The evaluation set is what makes this engineering.

Where tool-calling fits and where it does not, the protocol that is becoming the standard way to expose tools to models, and then the same shipping discipline as the first two projects.
weeks.deliverable: A working retrieval pipeline on pgvector with an evaluation set of at least twenty question-and-expected-source pairs, and a measured retrieval accuracy you can quote. · ALSO: PROJECT 3 LIVE — deployed with a demo account, guardrails and cost caps, a README stating measured retrieval accuracy and cost per query, and one MCP server exposing a Project 2 capability as a tool.
weeks.milestone: You can explain what an embedding is without hand-waving, and you have a number for how often your retrieval returns the right source. · AND: ANCHOR — Project 3 live by Saturday 7 March, with measured retrieval quality. Three shipped backend services, all linkable, all explainable line by line.

dsa.topic: Mixed mediums — timed → Mixed mediums — narrated aloud

weeks.title: HTML, CSS and Tailwind — Enough to Not Be Helpless + React — Enough to Demo Your Own APIs
weeks.theme:
One week on markup and layout. The goal is a clean, responsive page you built yourself, not a design career. Semantic HTML and flexbox will carry ninety per cent of what you ever need.

One week of React. Components, state, data fetching, forms, and an authenticated route. Enough to show your backends working and to answer React questions without bluffing.
weeks.deliverable: A responsive, accessible admin page for Project 2 built in Tailwind — navigation, a data table, a form — that works on a phone. · ALSO: A working admin interface for Project 2 — list, detail, create, edit, login, protected routes — reading live data, with loading, error and empty states handled everywhere.
weeks.milestone: You can build a two-column responsive layout from a blank file and explain what semantic HTML gives you beyond neatness. · AND: BLOCK IX CLOSES. You can demo all three services through an interface you built, and no screen renders undefined.

dsa.topic: Weak-area targeted set

weeks.title: Data Structures, Algorithms and Forty Problems + System Design, and Mock Loops With Real People
weeks.theme:
Not competitive programming. The specific patterns that appear in Pakistani technical rounds, solved unaided, out loud, under a clock — with forty-seven weeks of Saturday drills already behind you.

At three years you are not expected to design a global system. You are expected to reason out loud, ask about scale before designing for it, and justify a cache or a replica. You have built all of it — this week is learning to perform it.
weeks.deliverable: Forty problems solved unaided across the week, each with a written note on its pattern and complexity, plus a one-page pattern sheet in your own words. · ALSO: Four designs produced under a clock on one page each, a written script for the first five minutes of any design round, and at least three mock interviews with real people with written feedback.
weeks.milestone: ANCHOR approaches — forty problems unaided. Given an unseen medium problem you can name a plausible pattern within two minutes. · AND: ANCHOR — first mock with a real person on Monday 11 March. Three mocks done by Saturday, feedback written down and acted on.

dsa.topic: Full review — 40 problems across the week → Mock-format sets

weeks.title: Offers, Negotiation, and the Honest Accounting
weeks.theme: Two jobs this week. Convert whatever is in the pipeline, and decide honestly what happens next — because the plan closing is not the same as the search closing, and the worst outcome is drifting back to where you started.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: The audit — write down where you really are

tasks.text: Read Phase 0 Chapter 1 (How to Use This Book) and Chapter 2 (The Mission) end to end. Then start Chapter 4 (The AI Dependency Problem) — it is about you, and it is not an insult.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: The coding baseline — three problems, no help

tasks.text: Create the GitHub repository backend-mastery (public). Add LOG.md and BASELINE.md, commit, push. Then the coding baseline: three LeetCode Easy problems, twenty-five minutes each, no AI, no searching beyond language documentation. Record how many you finished unaided. If the answer is zero, write zero.

List ten target companies with backend teams. Start with: Arbisoft, Systems Ltd, 10Pearls, VentureDive, Devsinc, Tkxel, Motive, Careem, Folio3, Confiz. Find each careers page URL and write it into TARGETS.md.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: Values, types, and what === is really doing

tasks.text: Phase 1 Chapter 1 (JavaScript) — "Chapter Overview" and "Beginner Theory" in full. Focus on primitives versus objects, and why == and === behave differently. Write notes in your own words in LOG.md, not copied sentences.
Create a plain-text master CV file. List every project you touched in three years, one line each: what it did, what you did on it, and one number if you can find one.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: Coercion, by hand

tasks.text: No AI: write ten small functions that each demonstrate one type-coercion rule. Predict the output of each before running it. Every wrong prediction is the lesson — write down why you were wrong. Commit it.
Read Phase 10 Chapter 1 (Speaking About Your Work). Write a four-sentence answer to "What do you do at your current job?" Say it aloud three times. Record yourself once and listen back.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: Name the habit you are here to break

tasks.text: Finish Phase 0 Chapter 4. Then write in LOG.md the three specific things you have reached for AI to do in the last month that you could not do alone. Be exact — "wrote the SQL for the report screen", not "helped with backend". Those three lines are your syllabus.
Write your LinkedIn headline and About section as a draft. Headline formula: the role you want (Backend Engineer), your core stack, one proof point. Not "aspiring" anything.

days.weekTitle: The Honest Audit, and JavaScript You Actually Understand
days.focus: First build, first review

tasks.text: Deep build, two hours, no AI: a command-line contact book in plain Node — add, list, search, delete, saved to a JSON file. No framework, no packages. If you get stuck, read documentation and sit with it. This is the muscle.

Weekly review in LOG.md: how many days did I hit both blocks? Did I break the no-AI rule, and where? What do I understand today that I did not on Monday? Then read next week ahead.

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword

Read Phase 0 Chapter 3 (Beginner to Mastery Path). Write which of the five levels you are honestly at for JavaScript, and what evidence you have for that answer.

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword

days.weekTitle: Scope, Closures, and the this Keyword
days.focus: The var-in-a-loop problem
